lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
• In a solid, the molecules vibrate about their mean positions.
  • The molecules in a gas have random motion.
  • Temperature of a substance is the degree of hotness or coldness.
  • Heat is the energy in transit.
  • In the Kelvin scale, the temperature corresponding to the melting point of ice is 273 K.
  • The temperature which has the same value on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales is -40°. Let the common value be C = F = T. The conversion is F = (9/5) C + 32. Putting F = C = T gives T = (9/5) T + 32, so T - (9/5) T = 32, giving -(4/5) T = 32 and T = -40. So -40° is the same on both scales.
  • A better choice for a liquid in a liquid-in-glass thermometer is one that will expand linearly.
  • One disadvantage of using alcohol in a liquid-in-glass thermometer is that it wets the glass tube.
  • Water is not used as a thermometric liquid mainly due to its non-linear expansion.
  • A thermometer has a narrow capillary tube so that it gives a large change for a given temperature rise.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Solids: Fixed Shape and Volume

In a solid the particles are held close together by strong forces and can only vibrate about fixed mean positions; they cannot move past one another. The fixed arrangement of particles therefore keeps both the shape and the volume fixed.

Gases: No Fixed Shape or Volume

Gas particles are far apart, the forces between them are negligible, and they move freely and randomly at high speeds in all directions. Nothing holds them in fixed positions, so a gas spreads out to fill the whole container, taking the container's shape and volume.

Molecular Spacing in Solids, Liquids and Gases

In a solid the molecules are packed very closely together in a regular arrangement. In a liquid they are still close together but less regularly arranged and free to slide past one another. In a gas they are very far apart compared with their own size, with large empty spaces between them.

Effect of Heating a Liquid

Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the liquid's molecules, so they vibrate and move faster, push slightly further apart, and the liquid expands. If heating continues, more molecules gain enough energy to escape from the surface, so evaporation increases, and at the boiling point the liquid changes into vapour.

Temperature of a Body

The temperature of a body is the measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules, and it tells how hot or cold the body is. Two bodies at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium, and heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.

Heat as Energy in Transit

Heat is energy that flows from one body to another because of a temperature difference. It is called energy in transit because it exists only while it is flowing: a body does not contain heat, it contains internal energy, and heat is the name for internal energy on the move from a hotter body to a colder one.

Thermometric Property

A thermometric property is a physical property of a substance that changes regularly and measurably with temperature, so it can be used to measure temperature. Examples: the length of a mercury column in a glass tube, the volume of a gas at constant pressure, the pressure of a gas at constant volume, the electrical resistance of a metal wire, and the voltage produced by a thermocouple.

Temperature Scales

The three main scales are: the Celsius scale (ice point 0°C, steam point 100°C); the Fahrenheit scale (ice point 32°F, steam point 212°F); and the Kelvin scale, the SI scale (ice point 273 K, steam point 373 K). The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, 0 K = -273°C.

Sensitivity of a Thermometer

Sensitivity is how large a change the thermometer shows for a small change in temperature. A sensitive thermometer gives a large, easily read movement of its indicator, such as a long movement of the mercury thread, for even a small rise in temperature.

Linearity of a Thermometer

Linearity means that equal rises in temperature produce equal changes in the thermometric property, so the scale divisions are equally spaced. A linear thermometer can be calibrated with just two fixed points and read accurately anywhere between them; a non-linear thermometer needs many calibration points.

Accurate Thermometer Reading

An accurate reading needs a thermometer that is properly calibrated against fixed points, has a linear and sensitive thermometric property, and is given enough time to reach thermal equilibrium with the body being measured, with good thermal contact and no heat leaking away during the reading.

Direction of Heat Flow

The temperature difference determines the direction of heat flow: heat always flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature, never the other way by itself. The flow continues until both bodies reach the same temperature.

Heat and Internal Energy

Internal energy is the total energy stored in a body, the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its molecules; a body contains internal energy at all times. Heat is not stored in a body at all: it is energy in transit, flowing from a hotter body to a colder one because of a temperature difference. When heat flows into a body, the body's internal energy increases; when heat flows out, it decreases.

Feeling Cold on Touching

Energy travels from your hand to the cold surface. Cold is not a thing that flows; heat is energy in transit, and it always flows from the warmer body (your hand) to the colder body (the surface). The loss of energy from your hand is what you feel as coldness.

Feeling Your Own Fever

No, not reliably. Your hand and your forehead are both parts of your own body at nearly the same temperature, so almost no heat flows between them and your hand feels no clear difference. A thermometer, or another person's cooler hand, can detect the fever because a real temperature difference exists for heat to flow across.

lessons.title: Thinking Deeper
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic Theory and Plasma

Yes. Plasma is a fourth state of matter consisting of ionised gas: free electrons and positive ions moving randomly at high speeds. The kinetic molecular theory still applies, because it describes matter as particles in random motion whose average kinetic energy fixes the temperature; in plasma the particles are simply charged, and their collisions and electric forces are added to the picture. The Sun and the stars are matter in the plasma state, described by the same kinetic ideas.

Mercury Preferred over Alcohol

Mercury is preferred because it does not wet the glass tube, so the thread moves cleanly; it is opaque and shiny, so it is easy to see; it expands almost linearly with temperature; and it has a wide liquid range, from -39°C to 357°C, covering most everyday and laboratory temperatures. Alcohol wets the glass, is colourless and must be dyed, and boils at a low temperature, so it is used only for very low temperatures where mercury would freeze.

Water in Thermometers and 373 K Conversion

Water is unsuitable because its expansion is not linear: it expands unevenly, and between 0°C and 4°C it actually contracts as it warms, so the same thermometer reading could mean two different temperatures. It also wets the glass, is colourless and hard to see, and has a narrow liquid range for a thermometer. The equivalent of 373 K is 100°C on the Celsius scale (373 - 273) and 212°F on the Fahrenheit scale, the steam point of water.

Increasing Thermometer Sensitivity

Two ways: (1) make the capillary tube narrower, so the same expansion of liquid in the bulb pushes the thread much further along the tube; (2) make the bulb larger, so a given temperature rise expands a larger volume of liquid and drives the thread further. Using a liquid with a larger expansivity also increases sensitivity.

Heating Different Masses of Water

The rise will be 1°C. The stove supplies the same amount of heat in the same time, but the heat is now shared by twice the mass of water. Since temperature rise = heat supplied / (mass × specific heat capacity), doubling the mass halves the rise: 2°C / 2 = 1°C.

No Negative Kelvin Temperatures

The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, 0 K, the temperature at which the molecules of a substance have their minimum possible kinetic energy and cannot lose any more. No body can be colder than absolute zero, because kinetic energy cannot be negative, so no temperature below 0 K exists and the scale needs no negative numbers. 0 K equals -273°C.

A Thermometer Measures Its Own Temperature

The statement is true in an important sense. A thermometer does not directly read the temperature of the body it touches; it reads the temperature it itself reaches after exchanging heat with that body. Only when the thermometer has been in good contact long enough to reach thermal equilibrium with the body does its own temperature equal the body's temperature, and only then is its reading the body's temperature.

Touch and Temperature on a Winter Night

After a long winter night, all the objects have reached thermal equilibrium with the air, so they are all actually at the same temperature as the air. They feel different only because metals conduct heat away from your warm hand quickly and feel cold, while cotton, wood and plastic conduct heat slowly and feel warmer. Touch therefore judges how fast heat leaves your hand, not the true temperature; a thermometer would show all of them at the air temperature.

Comparing 1°C and 1°F Rises

An increase of 1°C is greater. One Celsius degree equals 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, because the Celsius scale has 100 divisions between the ice and steam points while the Fahrenheit scale has 180 divisions over the same interval. So a rise of 1°C is the same as a rise of 1.8°F, which is larger than a rise of 1°F.

Speeds of Gas Molecules

Gas molecules constantly collide with one another and with the walls, and in every collision energy is shared unequally: some molecules speed up and others slow down. The result is a spread of speeds, described by the Maxwell distribution, with most molecules near the average speed and a few much faster or much slower. Only the average speed is fixed by the temperature; individual speeds keep changing.

Temperature of a Vacuum

No, not in the usual sense. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles, and a perfect vacuum contains no particles at all, so it has no average kinetic energy to measure. We can speak of the temperature of the walls of a vacuum vessel, or of radiation passing through it, but the empty space itself has no temperature of its own.

A Hot Body Does Not Contain Heat

The statement is correct. Heat is energy in transit, flowing because of a temperature difference; it is not something stored inside a body. A hot body contains internal energy, the kinetic and potential energy of its molecules, which is large because its temperature is high. When it cools, it loses internal energy by giving out heat, but at no moment does it contain heat as a stored quantity.

The Sun as Matter

Yes, the Sun is matter. It is made of particles, mostly hydrogen and helium nuclei and free electrons, in the plasma state: a very hot, ionised gas. Plasma is a genuine state of matter, like solid, liquid and gas, with mass and volume, and the Sun's enormous mass holds it together by gravity. Being plasma does not stop it being matter; it is simply matter at extremely high temperature.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Particle Theory: Solids, Liquids and Gases

Particle theory says all matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion, with forces of attraction between them. In solids the particles are close together, strongly attracted, and vibrate about fixed positions, giving a fixed shape and volume. In liquids the particles are still close but the forces are weaker, so they can slide past one another: the volume stays fixed but the shape changes to fit the container. In gases the particles are far apart, the forces are negligible, and they move freely and randomly: neither shape nor volume is fixed, and the gas fills its container.

Temperature and the Mercury-in-Glass Thermometer

Temperature is the measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a body, telling how hot or cold it is. It is measured with a thermometer using a thermometric property that changes with temperature. A mercury-in-glass thermometer has a thin-walled glass bulb containing mercury, joined to a very narrow, uniform capillary tube sealed at the top, with a scale marked along the stem. When the bulb warms, the mercury expands and rises along the capillary; the position of the thread against the scale gives the temperature. The bulb is thin so heat reaches the mercury quickly, and the capillary is narrow so a small expansion gives a large, readable movement.

Comparing the Three Temperature Scales

The Celsius scale fixes the ice point at 0°C and the steam point at 100°C, with 100 equal divisions between them; it is the everyday scientific scale. The Fahrenheit scale fixes the ice point at 32°F and the steam point at 212°F, with 180 divisions between them; it is used mainly in a few countries for weather and daily life. The Kelvin scale is the SI scale: it starts at absolute zero, 0 K = -273°C, with the ice point at 273 K and the steam point at 373 K, and its divisions are the same size as Celsius degrees. Conversions: K = C + 273, and F = (9/5) C + 32.

Sensitivity, Range and Linearity

Sensitivity is the size of the thermometer's response to a small temperature change: a clinical thermometer is highly sensitive because its narrow capillary shows a large thread movement for a small fever change. Range is the interval of temperatures the thermometer can measure: a laboratory mercury thermometer ranges from about -39°C to 357°C, while a clinical thermometer covers only about 35°C to 42°C. Linearity means equal temperature rises give equal scale movements: mercury expands almost linearly, so its scale divisions are equal, whereas a thermometer using a property that changes unevenly would need unequal divisions and careful calibration.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example: Normal Body Temperature Conversion

The temperature of a normal human body on the Fahrenheit scale is 98.6°F. Convert it into Celsius scale and Kelvin scale.

Step 1: Celsius C = (F - 32) × 5/9 = (98.6 - 32) × 5/9 = 66.6 × 5/9 = 37°C.

Step 2: Kelvin K = C + 273 = 37 + 273 = 310 K.

Worked Example: Equal Celsius and Fahrenheit Reading

Find the temperature at which the Celsius and Fahrenheit thermometer readings would be the same.

Step 1: Let the common value be T, so C = F = T.

Step 2: F = (9/5) C + 32 becomes T = (9/5) T + 32.

Step 3: T - (9/5) T = 32, so -(4/5) T = 32, giving T = -40°.

Worked Example: Converting 5°F

Convert 5°F to Celsius and Kelvin scale.

Step 1: C = (5 - 32) × 5/9 = (-27) × 5/9 = -15°C.

Step 2: K = C + 273 = -15 + 273 = 258 K.

Worked Example: Converting 25°C

Find the equivalent temperature of 25°C on Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales.

Step 1: F = (9/5) × 25 + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77°F.

Step 2: K = 25 + 273 = 298 K.

Worked Example: Ungraduated Thermometer

The ice and steam points on an ungraduated thermometer are found to be 192 mm apart. Find the temperature on the Celsius scale if the length of the mercury thread is 67.2 mm above the ice point mark.

Step 1: The interval between ice point and steam point is 192 mm for 100°C.

Step 2: Temperature above the ice point = (length above ice point / total length) × 100 = (67.2/192) × 100.

Step 3: 67.2/192 = 0.35, so temperature = 0.35 × 100 = 35°C.

Worked Example: Temperature on the Fahrenheit Scale

The length between the fixed points of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is 20 cm. If the mercury level is 4.5 cm above the lower mark, find the temperature on the Fahrenheit scale.

Step 1: The fixed points are the ice point (32°F) and the steam point (212°F), a range of 180 Fahrenheit degrees over 20 cm.

Step 2: Fraction above the lower mark = 4.5/20 = 0.225.

Step 3: Temperature = 32 + 0.225 × 180 = 32 + 40.5 = 72.5°F.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
• Aluminium is not a magnetic material, unlike cobalt, iron and nickel, which are magnetic materials.
  • Magnetic lines of force enter into the south pole. Outside a magnet, magnetic lines of force leave the north pole and enter the south pole, then continue inside the magnet from south back to north, forming closed loops. They are curved, not always straight, and they never cross one another.
  • Permanent magnets cannot be made from soft iron. Soft iron is easily magnetised but loses its magnetism just as easily when the magnetising force is removed, so it can only make temporary magnets. Steel, neodymium and alnico retain their magnetism once magnetised, so they are used for permanent magnets.
  • Permanent magnets are used in a loudspeaker.
  • A common method used to magnetise a material is stroking.
  • Around a bar magnet, the correct compass directions are top arrow right, bottom arrow right, left arrow left, right arrow left. The field outside a magnet runs from its north pole to its south pole. To the left of the north pole the field points away from the magnet, to the left. To the right of the south pole the field points into the magnet, also to the left. Above the magnet the field lines travel from north to south, to the right, and below the magnet they also travel from the north side towards the south side, to the right.
  • A steel rod magnetised by the double touch stroking method becomes magnet AB with A = S, B = N. In the figure the two stroking magnets start at the centre of the bar and move outward: the left magnet carries its S pole in contact with the bar towards end A, and the right magnet carries its N pole in contact towards end B. In stroking, the end where a magnet finishes its stroke takes the same polarity as the stroking pole. So end A becomes S and end B becomes N.
  • The best material to protect a device from an external magnetic field is soft iron. Soft iron has a very high magnetic permeability, so magnetic flux prefers to travel through it rather than through air. A soft-iron casing therefore carries the external field around the device inside it instead of letting it pass through, shielding the device. Wood and plastic have no such effect, and steel retains magnetism, so soft iron is the best shield.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Temporary and Permanent Magnets

A temporary magnet is magnetised only while a magnetising force acts on it and loses its magnetism soon after the force is removed; soft iron is the usual material. A permanent magnet keeps its magnetism for a long time after being magnetised; steel, alnico and neodymium are the usual materials.

Magnetic Field of a Magnet

The magnetic field of a magnet is the region around it in which a magnetic force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. It is mapped by magnetic lines of force, which show both the direction and the relative strength of the field at each point.

Magnetic Lines of Force

Magnetic lines of force are imaginary lines used to picture a magnetic field. A compass needle placed on such a line points along it. Their properties are: they leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet; they never cross one another; they are crowded together where the field is strong and spread apart where it is weak; and they always form closed loops through the inside of the magnet.

Uses of Permanent Magnets and Electromagnets

Permanent magnets are used in compasses, loudspeakers, electric motors and generators, refrigerator door seals, and magnetic toys. Electromagnets, whose magnetism can be switched on and off, are used in electric cranes for lifting scrap iron, electric bells, relays and circuit breakers, magnetic separators, and the cores of transformers and motors.

Magnetic Field of a Current-Carrying Long Coil

A current-carrying long coil, or solenoid, produces a magnetic field like that of a bar magnet: the field inside the coil is strong and nearly uniform, with parallel lines running from one end to the other, and the field outside loops back from the north-seeking end to the south-seeking end. The polarity of the ends is fixed by the direction of the current.

lessons.title: Thinking Deeper
lessons.notes_html:
Stored Bar Magnets and Their Keepers

In the figure the left magnet is shown with its upper half red and its lower half blue, and the right magnet with its upper half blue and its lower half red. Taking red as north and blue as south, the left magnet has its N pole at the top and its S pole at the bottom, while the right magnet has its S pole at the top and its N pole at the bottom, so unlike poles face each other across the top and the bottom. P and Q, the bars laid across the tops and bottoms of the two magnets, are soft-iron keepers: they join the opposite poles and close the magnetic circuit, which stops the magnets from losing their magnetism during storage.

Magnetising a Steel Bar in a Solenoid

Circuit diagram to draw: a solenoid drawn as a horizontal coil with the steel bar AB lying inside it along its axis, a battery connected to the ends of the coil through a switch, and the current direction marked. To make end A (the left end) a north pole, the current viewed from the A end must flow anticlockwise, by the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current and the thumb points to the north pole. So wire the battery so that current enters the coil at the B end side and circulates anticlockwise as seen from A; label end A as N, end B as S, and mark the battery terminals and the current arrows on the coil.

Like Poles and a Compass in the Gap

The two facing ends must be like poles. Justification: if the facing ends were unlike poles, the field in the gap would point straight across the gap from the north pole to the south pole, and the compass needle would settle pointing across the gap, east-west. Instead the needle settles north-south, the direction of the Earth's own field, which means the two magnets' fields cancel each other at the middle of the gap. That cancellation happens only when the facing ends are like poles, both north or both south, pushing equal fields against each other. Field lines to draw: lines leaving each facing north pole (or entering each facing south pole) and curving away, meeting and cancelling at the centre, with the compass needle drawn north-south at the centre. Note: the needle alone proves the facing poles are alike, but it cannot by itself tell whether they are both north or both south.

Electromagnetic Induction

Yes, the reverse process is true and is called electromagnetic induction. When the magnetic field through a coil changes, a current is induced in the coil. Example: a generator or dynamo. A coil rotated between the poles of a magnet experiences a continuously changing magnetic field, so a current is induced in the coil and can light a bulb or charge a battery. Moving a bar magnet in and out of a coil has the same effect: the galvanometer needle deflects while the magnet moves and returns to zero when it stops, showing that only a changing field induces a current.

Four Solenoids Around a Centre

Diagram to draw: four solenoids A, B, C and D placed at the left, bottom, right and top of a circle around centre O, each with its axis pointing at O, and each wound so that its inner end facing O is a north pole; mark the current direction in each coil accordingly (anticlockwise as seen from O for each inner end).

Explanation: each solenoid's field at O points radially outward, away from its own north pole, and the four equal outward fields cancel one another, so the net field at O is zero with all solenoids on. When one solenoid, say D at the top, is switched off, its outward (downward) contribution disappears, and the remaining three fields no longer cancel: their net field points in the opposite direction to the missing contribution, that is upward, towards the switched-off solenoid D. The same argument holds for whichever solenoid is switched off.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Identifying a Magnet or a Magnetic Material

Suspend the object freely: a magnet always settles pointing roughly north-south, while an unmagnetised magnetic material has no preferred direction. Bring a known magnet near it: a magnet is repelled by a like pole of the known magnet, while a mere magnetic material is only ever attracted, never repelled. Repulsion is therefore the sure test: attraction alone cannot distinguish a magnet from a magnetic material, because a magnet attracts both magnets and magnetic materials.

Field Strength and Lines of Force

The strength of a magnetic field at a point is shown by how crowded the magnetic lines of force are there: closely spaced lines mean a strong field, widely spaced lines mean a weak field, and parallel, equally spaced lines mean a uniform field. Diagrams to draw: (1) a bar magnet with lines crowded near the poles and spreading out further away, showing the field is strongest at the poles; (2) two like poles facing each other, with lines bending away from the gap, showing repulsion and zero field at the middle; (3) a uniform field drawn as parallel, equally spaced straight lines, as inside a long solenoid. In each diagram label where the field is strong and where it is weak.

What a Magnet Attracts

Taken literally the statement is not complete, and it should be read as: a magnet attracts only magnetic materials. A magnet attracts iron, nickel, cobalt and other ferromagnetic materials, whether or not they are already magnets, because it first induces magnetism in them and then attracts them. It does not attract non-magnetic materials such as wood, plastic, aluminium or copper. The statement is therefore true only in the sense that attraction is limited to magnetic substances; a magnet does not attract everything, and repulsion, not attraction, is the test that proves another body is itself a magnet.
